name: HIAS: US advocacy and litigation for refugees
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees waiting abroad for US resettlement, by the largest nationalities admitted in recent years (the DRC, Afghanistan, Venezuela, Syria, Myanmar, Sudan, Somalia, Ukraine); a judgment.
summary: HIAS spends about $3 million a year (our estimate, inside its US accounts line) on US advocacy, community engagement and litigation, chiefly as a plaintiff in Pacito v. Trump against the January 2025 suspension of refugee admissions, which forced the admission of a few hundred approved refugees in 2025. We value the pending case as a small chance (6%) of restoring about 50,000 admissions a year for the years a win counts, and the 2025 admissions as won, each refugee gaining the US level of consumption over decades against the level where they wait, with HIAS credited 15% of the litigation; at HIAS's own next-dollar figure (49%) it comes to about 1.9 years of healthy life per $1,000. It is more than ten times its peers because a refugee resettled in the US gains several doublings of consumption for decades, so even a small chance of restoring tens of thousands of admissions is worth a lot; the result is mostly uncertainty (the chance of success, HIAS's share and the years a win counts span a thousandfold), and it is discounted for missing data.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled programme cost in fiscal 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), with its share of management and fundraising, from HIAS's audited consolidated accounts. Donated legal services, booked in the accounts at the law firms' rates, are not HIAS's own money: they enter the credit share, not the cost.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, delivery falling short and missing outcome data. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction) and put into healthy years by its unit's conversion, so each moves only with its own sliders.

Extra refugees admitted to the US a year if the suspension is overturned
rows.explainer: The US admitted about 100,000 refugees in fiscal 2024 and set 7,500 for fiscal 2026 (annual report p. 9). A win in Pacito v. Trump, the class action against the suspension, would restore part of the programme, which courts have so far narrowed to refugees already approved. 50,000 a year (20,000-100,000). Our judgment.

rows.label: Chance the suspension is overturned by the litigation and advocacy HIAS joins
rows.explainer: The district court enjoined the suspension in February 2025, but the Ninth Circuit stayed most of the injunction and the Supreme Court has sided with the administration in most immigration stays in 2025. One event, drawn as happens or doesn't. 6% (2-15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years a win counts
rows.explainer: The site's one number of years a won reform brings a change forward (docs/normalization.md 2.9): a later administration might restore admissions anyway.

rows.label: Years until a win takes effect
rows.explainer: Appeals and rebuilding the overseas processing pipeline take a year or more. 1 year (0.5-3). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: Refugees start on resettlement cash and benefits and most work within months; a few years on they earn around the poorest fifth's level, 45% of the average per household (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024). 40% (30-55%) over their years. Our judgment.

rows.label: Refugees' consumption where they wait, as a share of the host country's average
rows.explainer: Refugees referred for resettlement wait in camps and cities in East Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America, mostly below their hosts. 60% (40-90%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Refugees' consumption while waiting (PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: Kenya, Uganda and Honduras stand in for the host countries (a judgment).

rows.label: Years a resettled refugee gains in the US
rows.explainer: Refugees admitted are of every age, many children; without resettlement most would stay displaced for decades (protracted situations average over 20 years). 30 years (15-45). Our judgment.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per refugee admitted, discounted over their years
rows.explainer: Each year's cohort of extra refugees gains the US level against the level where they wait, every year they stay, on the site's log-income scale.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per refugee (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Zero: the gain is counted as income; safety and family reunion are in the unmodelled shares, so they aren't counted twice.

rows.label: Illness averted per refugee admitted, in healthy years
rows.explainer: Better treatment of chronic and infectious illness in the US than in camps and poor cities, over the years in the US: 0.02 healthy years per refugee (0-0.1), apart from the income and the mortality rows. Our judgment.

rows.label: Excess yearly mortality where refugees wait, over the US (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Crude death rates in long-running camps sit near or above their hosts' (Kenya and Uganda about 0.5-0.6% a year for young populations, UN WPP) against far lower age-specific rates in the US for the same young people. 0.2 points a year (0-0.5). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted under five
rows.explainer: Children are about 40% of refugees (UNHCR) and young children die at higher rates in camps, while adults far outnumber them over decades in the US. 30% (10-45%). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: 20,400 people contacted their representatives 41,600 times, 284 congregations held Refugee Shabbat and vigils ran in 14 states (annual report p. 12): goodwill toward refugees beyond the litigation. +5% (0 to +15%). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: Litigation and protest can harden opposition. -1% (-5% to 0). Our judgment.
